title: Ops Lab: Request Journey Sleuth Walkthrough - Asterion Labs
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Asterion through the Console request-journey sleuthing workflow: tracing, request logs, playback, KV/prefix cache investigation, and failover policies. Discussed security (SOC2, SAML, KMS), deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC), and a proposed pilot to validate p99 latency and error rate under their traffic. Agreed next steps for security paperwork, pilot setup, and sample payload share.
action_items: Maya Chen - Send security whitepaper and SOC2 summary - 2027-02-16
Liam O'Connor - Provision sandbox pilot cluster and run baseline P95/P99 runs - 2027-02-21
Ravi Patel - Share representative payloads, traffic distribution and expected TPS - 2027-02-18
Eva Morales - Confirm scope for audit logs and retention requirements - 2027-02-18
next_steps: Send security docs and SOC2 artifacts
Schedule pilot run and invite customer SREs
Provide sandbox console access and a short how-to deck
Share dedicated vs hosted pricing and SLAs
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-02-14 14:30 UTC | Duration: ~52m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Ravi (Asterion Head of Platform), Eva (SRE), Jordan (PM)

Summary line: quick demo of Console's request sleuth / playback / trace correlation + discussion of pilot and security.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you taking the time today. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Ravi: Hi, Ravi here.
[00:07] Eva: Eva.
[00:09] Jordan: Jordan.
[00:10] Liam: Liam from Redwood.
[00:12] Maya: Great. I'll share my screen, we'll run through a few real request traces, show playback and the KV cache fallthroughs, and then leave time for Q&A and pilot planning.
[00:25] Jordan: Sounds good, our main goal today is to understand how we would debug a user-facing error chain — like when the assistant returns hallucinated PII or times out mid-response.
[00:35] Maya: Totally, that's the core use case we see. Okay share screen now. Let me pull up an example trace.
[00:45] [screen share noise]
[00:50] Maya: Alright, here's the request timeline view. On the top we have the high-level request, then the per-stage timings: routing, cache lookup, model execution, streaming handoff. You can click a segment to see span-level logs.
[01:05] Liam: One thing to call out — our trace id is propagated through the system. So if you're on Dedicated or Private you still get the same correlator in your logs. Sometimes the agent transcription renders it as speaker one, but in the console it's the actual trace id.
[01:20] Ravi: When you say cache lookup, is that the prefix/KV cache? We use a lot of short prompts and want to avoid repeated generation cost.
[01:28] Maya: Yes that's the prefix + KV cache. In this trace you can see the prefix cache hit metric and the kv-fallback rate. Notice here we have a 10% fallthrough because the cache keys differ by a subtle tokenization mismatch.
[01:45] Eva: Tokenization mismatch — can we see the raw prompt text?
[01:48] Liam: Yes, click the request payload panel. Warning: our redaction heuristics sometimes obfuscate PII, and auto-transcription can label things oddly — e g 'kay vee cache' or 'K V cache' in the generated notes. But the stored request shows the actual bytes unless you've turned on full retention controls.
[02:10] Jordan: About retention — we need logs for 13 months for compliance, is that supported?
[02:16] Maya: Yes, for Private deployments we support configurable retention and long-term audit log export to your S3 or GCS. For hosted, we have enterprise retention add-ons. We'll include the specifics in the security docs.
[02:30] Ravi: Okay. Show the replay flow — how do we reproduce a particular failure?
[02:35] Maya: In the console you can select a trace and hit 'Replay'. That spawns a sandboxed request through the same model version and routing policy, with the option to inject the same KV cache state or force cold-start.
[02:50] Liam: For these replays we capture the model variant, quantization profile, and approx batch context. Small note: replays won't replicate non-deterministic sampling exactly, but they reproduce the same model state and routing pathways so you can debug infrastructure causes.
[03:05] Eva: Does replay let us toggle fallback to smaller model or different region? We sometimes see fallbacks kick in during traffic spikes and want to test that behavior.
[03:14] Liam: Yup, you can override routing policy at replay time — force route to hosted, dedicated, or to a lower-cost variant. The UI also surfaces why fallback occurred: saturation, error budget, or region health.
[03:27] Jordan: Can the console correlate application logs with request traces? Our product logs are in DataDog.
[03:32] Maya: We have integrations with Datadog, Splunk, and ELK. You can attach an external log link via trace metadata. The console shows a per-request 'linked logs' panel that opens your external logs filtered by trace id.
[03:48] Ravi: Nice. Another question on security — SSO and roles: we need SCIM and SAML.
[03:54] Maya: We support SAML SSO with SCIM provisioning and role-based access control. For private deployments you can map to your LDAP or Okta groups. We'll send the SAML config doc.
[04:06] Eva: KMS integration? We want customer-managed keys.
[04:09] Liam: Yes, KMS/HSM options on Private and Dedicated tiers. Hosted supports envelope encryption with customer KMS where required. Again, that's in the security pack.
[04:22] Jordan: Going back to traces — show an error chain where model timed out and the client saw partial output.
[04:28] Maya: Here's one. You can see streaming started at 0.8s, then there was a model preemption at 1.9s — our runtime threw a transient GPU OOM on that shard, then we retried on a different instance and resumed. The console shows retry count and the portion of response that was streamed.
[04:50] Eva: How is partial output handled? Do you get a flag that the response is incomplete?
[04:54] Liam: Yes the request status includes final_state: completed | partial | failed. For partial we attach the last token offset and the resume token. Apps can call the resume endpoint to fetch continuation.
[05:07] Maya: In many apps you can also configure automatic fallback to a stateless small model so the user still gets something while continuity is resolved. But we surface that as a policy decision with cost tradeoffs.
[05:20] Ravi: Our SLOs are p99 generation under 800ms, and p95 under 300ms, for short prompts. Can Redwood hit that?
[05:28] Liam: Depends on model and your dedicated capacity. On Dedicated with optimized kernels and batching tuned for your distribution, we've hit sub-400ms p99 on similar workloads. We'll run baseline numbers in the pilot to show realistic p95/p99.
[05:42] Jordan: Can you show the latency breakdown per token?
[05:45] Maya: Yep — here's the token-by-token timing chart. You can see network decode, model compute, and queueing. In this trace the queueing spiked during a short burst. The console will show correlated autoscale events and whether burst capacity was consumed.
[06:05] Ravi: If we see a KV cache miss pattern like earlier, can we generate a suggested config?
[06:10] Liam: Yeah, Optimize suggests cache key normalization and tokenization tuning — e.g., normalize whitespace, use sentence-level keys, or a lemmatized key for high variance prompts. The console shows an expected hit rate delta if you apply the suggestion.
[06:24] Maya: Quick note on mis-transcriptions — some of the auto notes might say 'latency if you batch too much' and transcribe it weirdly; always trust the raw trace panels for exact numbers.
[06:35] Jordan: We have a compliance question: do you provide immutable audit logs for every request?
[06:40] Maya: Yes, we can store append-only audit logs with integrity checks and export to your object store. For Private deployments we can also run in air-gapped mode.
[06:52] Eva: For the pilot, we want to test a mixed workload with long-form completions and short-chat messages. Can we configure traffic shaping?
[06:58] Liam: You can replay real traffic profiles via the pilot harness. We'll ingest the provided payloads and run them across the same sequence of requests, measuring p95/p99, cache hit rate, and cost per request.
[07:12] Maya: If there are no more security Qs I'll show a tricky example where a prompt produced PII.
[07:17] Ravi: We have to be strict on PII.
[07:19] Liam: In this trace the moderation hook fired. You can see the moderation span and the action: either redact, fail safe, or route to human review. The console lets you tune the moderation threshold per route.
[07:33] Jordan: How customizable is the moderation pipeline?
[07:36] Maya: You can insert custom rules or external classifiers; we provide hooks to call your internal moderation service and annotate requests.
[07:45] [Performance lag in screen share]
[07:52] Maya: Sorry slight lag — continuing. Here's a request where the KV cache key mismatched due to punctuation. If you expand the key diff you'll see the tokenization mismatch — one had an em-dash replaced by two hyphens.
[08:08] Eva: Oof. Are there tools to normalize keys automatically?
[08:11] Liam: Yes Optimize suggests normalizers, and you can enable on-the-fly normalization in the proxy layer. That can improve hit rates significantly but you should validate for semantics.
[08:23] Ravi: About dedicated capacity pricing — can you give high level?
[08:27] Maya: We'll send the detailed pricing sheet, but at a high level Dedicated is a flat monthly for reserved GPU slices plus per-request unit discounts. The pilot will let us estimate effective unit cost for your workload.
[08:40] Jordan: For the replay, if we recreate a failure that depends on external context (like a DB lookup) can we stub that out?
[08:47] Liam: Replays can inject mock context or point to your test endpoints; we have a 'context override' panel. That helps reproduce errors caused by downstream services.
[09:00] Maya: Okay I'm going to trigger a replay for this failing trace and toggle the KV state to cold-start so you can see the model path.
[09:08] [Replay runs — console shows logs streaming]
[09:15] Liam: See here the model selection hit a high-tail cost and we retried on a smaller quantized variant before failing. That explains the partial output.
[09:28] Eva: So the console shows the exact step where the fallback happened, nice.
[09:31] Maya: Yep, and you can export the full step-by-step timeline as JSON to attach to your ticketing system.
[09:39] Jordan: Any rate limits we should know about?
[09:41] Liam: For Hosted there are per-account QoS limits and we recommend gateway throttles. On Dedicated you can set precise per-route quotas. We'll include recommended throttling configs for your use case.
[09:54] Ravi: Our infra team will want to run the pilot in our VPC for the first week. Is that supported?
[09:59] Maya: We can do a Private or VPC-hosted pilot; it depends on how isolated you want the control plane. We often run an initial Dedicated pilot with a VPC peering setup. We'll propose options in writing.
[10:12] Jordan: Timeline — we'd like to decide by the end of next week. Is that feasible?
[10:16] Maya: Yes if we get the sample payloads and approvals, we can spin up sandbox in under a week. Liam will provision and run baseline tests.
[10:25] [Short silence as notes are taken]
[10:30] Maya: Any other questions?
[10:33] Eva: One last: do you keep request diffs when we redact PII to prove compliance?
[10:38] Liam: We keep an audit trail: original hash, redaction transform record, and the redacted payload. For Private deployments you can disable raw retention entirely.
[10:48] Jordan: Great.
[10:49] Maya: Ok quick recap and next steps: I'll send the security pack and SOC2 summary by Tuesday. Liam will provision a sandbox pilot and run P95/P99 baselines once we get payloads. Ravi and Eva will share payload samples and audit scope. We'll also send a pricing sheet for Dedicated vs Hosted.
[11:10] Ravi: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[11:12] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.
[11:15] [meeting ends]

Notes on transcription quality: some proper nouns and acronyms mis-transcribed in auto-notes; ground truth is in attached artifacts which Maya will send.

References mentioned: security pack link (to be shared), pricing spreadsheet (to be shared), pilot checklist (to be shared).
